utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. No preliminaries were announced which means that we can immediately continue. Mr. Lukic, is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, we are. We are calling Mr. Bozidar Krnojelac via videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then let's establish whether the videolink is functioning well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We can hear you and we can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear you and we can see you as well. We'll start with a solemn declaration by the witness. Witness, please remain seated. But we'd like you to make the solemn declaration of which the text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krnojelac. You will first be examined by Mr. Lukic. I hope you can see him. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please give your name and surname for the record?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: My name is Bozidar Krnojelac. My father's name is Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At one point in time, did you give a written statement to representatives of the Defence of General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the representative of the Registry please give him a copy of his statement so that he can have it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the first page of this statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the signature on that first page?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: It's my very own.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last page now. Do you see a signature there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: It is the same signature, my very own, once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you the following: If I were put the same questions to you today as those put by my colleagues, would you basically give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We could like to tender Mr. Krnojelac's statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the number of the document. You didn't raise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly, because we didn't have it on our screen so I was dealing only with the hard copy. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I could perhaps help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could it be 1D1653.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour that's exactly the number of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we -- you've asked whether the witness would give the same answers. Witness, having read the statement, are the answers you have given in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I here of no objections. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D650, Your Honours. 6-5-0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D650 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I would just read the statement summary of this witness, and I would have a couple of questions with your leave at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness has been informed about the purpose of reading the summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Krnojelac, Bozidar was born on the 8th of December in 1967 in Foca and before war in BiH he worked in Maglic company. He is a war veteran and invalid. Witness will testify how incidents during strike in Focatrans company led to ethnic division of Muslims and Serbs. Intervention from special police forces in company led to repression towards Serbs. Witness will testify how both ethnic groups, Serbs and Muslims, were armed themselves, how Crisis Staff existed on both sides, Serbian led by Miro Stanic and Muslims by Saimpasic. Serbian people in Foca self-organised due to necessity to defend themselves, while armed conflict in Foca began on the 8th of April 1992, with attack from Muslim side. Due to clashes, Muslim civilians were leaving Foca along with their armed groups. Witness was engaged in village guards, along with his brothers. He was in Nikolic's unit. He will explain his father's role in the KP Dom Foca, and he will testify that his father was appointed by Foca Municipal Crisis Staff. The situation in Foca was chaotic and out of any control. Some individuals wanted revenge for crimes committed by Muslims, while there were many individuals or groups which could not be controlled or influenced, either by civilian or military authorities. That was the statement summary and I would have couple more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you please draw my attention to where it exactly says that the intervention from special police forces in the company led to repression towards Serbs. Where do we find that exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 3, but I will have couple more questions on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, okay, but where do we find that it led to repression against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I have couple of more questions. We need some explanations on this since we heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- the same evidence from other witnesses in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you're summarising this statement, whatever additional questions you may have, I think I'm entitled to ask you where we find that specific portion of what you made public as a summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is that I'm actually summarising the testimony of this witness not only the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can't summarise anything we haven't heard yet. You're supposed to summarise the statement as we -- as it was put before us and not to anticipate on evidence you still expect to be given. Do I understand therefore your answer to be what you read as a summary is not yet found in the statement in paragraph 3 as far as repression against Serbs is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, then, understood, and I would like to invite you next time to limit yourself to what we have received in the statement itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from any additional questions you may put to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krnojelac, you heard this. You heard what the Trial Chamber had to say in respect of the brief remarks I made just now. It is your statement that is evidence and what you will say by way of testimony so what I say is not evidence. So now let us move on to paragraph 3. It's about what happened in Focatrans. Can you tell us briefly what happened in Focatrans?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have trouble understanding what the witness is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I seek the assistance of Madam Registrar at the other side of the videolink so as to ensure that the witness is speaking loud enough and that the microphone is close enough to him for the interpreters in The Hague to hear what he says.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I have brought the microphone closer to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Witness, you are asked whether you could tell us what happened in Focatrans.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I started by making an introduction. It was a transportation company for transporting passengers and goods, and both Serbs and Muslims worked there normally, and there was a misunderstanding between the director and the Serb side and he -- and he, I mean, how do I put this? He treated his colleagues better than Serbs and then they went on strike, and then in fact this was a -- an incident at republican level. And special units were called in, special forces to suppress this strike. And then this incident occurred; namely, that they removed the Serbs to one side and then there was this clash between the police and these Serb forces, I mean these Serb people in town, and indeed they applied force. Mr. Vikic's special forces did. And there were other police from elsewhere, so it wasn't only special forces. There were also police from elsewhere. So that indeed caused revolt and divisions between the Serb and Muslim populations in Foca. It went on for a few days. It wasn't just one day. It went on for several days. How do I put this? Gatherings were not allowed. More than three persons could not move about together. Every night, shops and other establishments were searched, so life basically became impossible in town. And then this D-Day came, if I can put it that way, and then they pushed the entire population that went out into town that day towards the bus station. And then, of course, there was quite a bit of commotion. There were a lot of people who were in the streets, and then they started beating us up and all of these things then happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you whether you personally had anything to do with what was happening?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I was right by the bus station when the beatings started and the tear gas and the hitting and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move to paragraph 4 briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You speak about arming of both peoples.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any direct knowledge about arming, and if so what is that knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Direct knowledge precisely, because I worked as a waiter in a restaurant and there were quite a few people who would come there. And generally speaking, it is in restaurants and coffee bars that people talk about most things. And then I had contacts on both sides, and I heard this talk about both Muslims and Serbs being armed. It was the SDS that was arming the Serbs and the SDA that was arming the Muslims. So I know, Saimpasic, Sajo, was mentioned, and we all know him very well. He had some fruit and vegetable shops in Foca. And what they did, I think, was perfectly normal. The two sides secured their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 6 now. You say that the Serb population in Foca started to organise themselves by forming village guards?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As for this self-organisation, who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Again, it was the political parties and the leaders of the parties in the SDA and the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, was there a Crisis Staff that had been established on the Muslim side, on the Serb side, and can you tell us where these Crisis Staffs were?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: On the eve of the war, yes, I cannot say whether it was a month or two or three months beforehand. The Muslims had a Crisis Staff and the Serbs had a Crisis Staff. The Muslim Crisis Staff was in Focatrans and the Serb Crisis Staff was in Cerezluk in a private home. I don't know whose house it was, but I know that it was in this privately owned house for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the same Focatrans?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: It is one and the same company. At the station, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 now, please. You say that your house burned down during the fighting. When did the fighting break out in Foca? We already have that in paragraph 6. You say on the 8th of April there was the first major armed conflict and then you were -- actually, how long were you in your house?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: On the 8th, sometime, say, around 10.00 or 11.00, the first shooting was heard. I was in the house and there was a lull in the shooting. I was there until the 11th and then we moved out of the house because we realised that all the other Serb houses had been left and we went to Cerezluk where Arsenije and Sretenije, my uncles have houses. That's where we went. And my house was torched. Later on when the Muslims were withdrawing -- actually, if necessary I can explain why we moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: There was this old school, Ivan Goran Kovacic, by my house that had been moved to another location; that is to say, it had been abandoned. Now, that is where the Muslim units gathered. Some wore green berets and that's why we called them green berets. Probably there were people from elsewhere as well. Then they started gathering there, that institution, and then we felt insecure. Quite simply we were afraid for our own lives, and on the evening of the 11th we went to Cerezluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when your house was torched, do you have any information?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Two or three days later, when they were withdrawing towards the exit, if I can put it that way, Donje Polje and the bridge, the other bridge by the KP Dom, and they withdrew towards Gorazde, the population, the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Two or three days later, could you explore with the witness two or three days after what, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, you've heard Judge Orie. Three or four days later, after what? After the conflict broke out or after you left?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: After I left the house. Of course the house was not torched while we were there. It was torched after we left. I mean if the gentleman did not understand what I was saying, well, the Presiding Judge. When we [as interpreted] were withdrawing, because Muslim forces control that area, so during the withdrawal it wasn't only my house that was torched but 10 or 12 other ethnic Serb homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Only I would correct the transcript at page 10, line 24, it says "when we were withdrawing." The witness was all the time talking about the withdrawal of Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can seek to have it verified but you can't change the transcript, Mr. Lukic. But you can verify whether the transcript accurately reflects what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The witness already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I was just going to ask that what the witness said during that exchange be reflected on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But I can -- since it's not in the transcript, I can ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness when other people are speaking and when other microphones are on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, as I was speaking what did you actually say?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I did not say that we were withdrawing. I was saying that the Muslim forces were withdrawing. We were moving out. We moved out of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then ask for some clarification. You say you moved out or you had moved out because it was three days after you had moved out that your house was burning, was put on fire. And you are talking about the Muslims withdrawing at that point in time. Does that mean that you had moved out, Muslims were withdrawing, that the space was therefore more or less empty or at least not occupied by either Muslims or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would really have to ask you now which place you have in mind, my house or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you had moved out from where you lived. The Muslims withdrawing put your house on fire --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but they were withdrawing -- let me be clear. They did not withdraw that day when we moved out. I said two or three days later, after that fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not contesting that in any way. My question was: Does that mean that you had moved out, the Muslims a couple of days later withdrew. Does that mean that the area where your house was was under control of none of the parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say that it was no-man's land. It was the territory held by Muslims, but my house was empty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you also tell us that they withdrew. And my understanding is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three days after the fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When your house was set on fire, were other houses set on fire too?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I've already said another 10 or 12 houses were torched, precisely -- that's an area where the boundary is, the boundary with the Muslim majority area under the Celovina hill, that's approximately the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not on the record, to whom did these torched houses belong?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: They were all Serb houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Judge wanted to know at one point when the Muslims were withdrawing after three or four days of fighting.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those houses were torched. So for a while was this area empty? How did the Muslims know that Serbs had moved out of that area?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: There was fighting. The area was not empty. And as the Serbs advanced, the Muslims were withdrawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened with the majority of the Muslim civilian population?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: We have to go back to the beginning at this point. Just before the fighting began, before the 8th of April, perhaps a month before that there was already talk that a conflict was afoot but nobody knew exactly what would happen. And the Muslims and Serbs went back to the villages where they had come from. Some people had come back to their villages and those who stayed, everybody listened to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It seems that we lost the connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I verify with representatives of the registry on both sides whether the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will wait for a second to see whether it can be re-established. Madam Registrar on the other side, could you confirm that you can hear and see us again? We don't hear you at this moment, although we can see you. Madam Registrar, could you speak a few words so as to see whether the audio connection is functioning? Until now, we have not heard anything. If you can hear me, could you just check that your microphone on your side is switched on. Could we check again whether the audio is now functioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the system will be restarted. We're still waiting for the connection to be functional again, but apparently nothing happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a short break. Everyone is requested to remain standby until the connection has been re-established. We take the break not sine die but sine hora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we establish whether the videolink is functioning again? Could you confirm that --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can hear you and we can see you from this side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can see you, we can hear you. Mr. Lukic may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krnojelac, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you when the Muslim forces were withdrawing from Foca, what happened with the majority of the population, the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You started speaking about it extensively. The people from Foca, did they start moving with the Muslim forces that were from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Can I give a more extensive explanation because I really need to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We haven't got much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think it's probably a little bit late now but the question appears leading to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You started giving us an extensive explanation?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Extensive remarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tell us briefly then what happened with civilians of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I started telling you about it. I started saying how in the first part, part of them went to their villages. The part that remained, we all listened to the media, we had reporters who were saying that over 5.000 Serb Chetniks were coming, and of course this revolted and intimidated the Muslim people, so they withdrew towards Gorazde with their own units. That's it briefly. The journalist's name is Semso Tucakovic. He made statements like that and they were absolutely incorrect. So he just created more confusion and people were terrified, but really there were no such units and it was very few. Well, this wasn't your question but there were very few people there who came from the Serb guard and the White Eagles. And he was exaggerating as if it's 5.000. There aren't 5.000 people in Foca who could fight let alone 5.000 volunteers and Serb Chetniks as he called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Once you've mentioned Semso Tucakovic. Tell us what was his ethnicity and where did he broadcast from?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Well, I think from the name it's obvious he was Muslim. Whether he was from Sarajevo or somewhere else, I don't know, but he certainly wasn't broadcasting from Foca. He may have been getting his information from elsewhere, from outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. One or two questions to clarify. How many White Eagles were there and how many Serb guards members were there? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a question for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm sure there were no more than 100, certainly not over a hundred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how did you know? Did you see them? What's the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw both of them, both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The White Eagles were at the KP Dom and the Serb guards were in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you see them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I saw them at the beginning of the war, after the 20th of April onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will pick up on what Judge Orie just asked and it has to do with paragraph 9 of your statement. Did you personally go to the KP Dom, to the penitentiary facility, and in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I went to the KP Dom in the capacity of protecting my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the role of the White Eagles whom you said you saw around the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: When I got there to the KP Dom, they were already inside and they were already holding some prisoners. They were in the compound, in the inner compound of the KP Dom when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did they wear?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: They had the White Eagle insignia on the left sleeve, the uniform was camouflage, some of them had caps, others didn't. Those who had caps had a cockade on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did they have JNA insignia?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who was bringing prisoners into the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: The Serb guards and men from the Territorial Defence. The general population, I don't know in what capacity they operated. People from the Territorial Defence, but mainly the Serb guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it correct also that you said the White Eagles had prisoners in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. When I arrived with my father after the 20th, there were already some prisoners in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, you said you went on from the 20th of April to the KP Dom. You saw White Eagles and Serb guards there. That was well after or was it at the time the Muslim population was leaving or had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslims had left. Most of the Muslims had left the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, how many Serb guards or White Eagles there were which, as you said erroneously, led them to leave, you did not see before they left the White Eagles or the Serb guards. Could you confirm that or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that they were there even before because when I left my home, went to Cerezluk, the Serb guards were there and I also found them in the KP Dom. I don't know when the White Eagles arrived but the Serb guards were already in Foca on the 11th, that I know, maybe they had arrived even earlier, I can't be sure, but on the 11th they were certainly there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you earlier told us that at the most there was 100. How could you know that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than 100, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But how did you know that well before the 20th or did you travel through the area? What made you know that there were not more than 100.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left my home on the 11th and went to Cerezluk. I saw them up there. I met them there. They had uniforms with the lettering "Serb guards" on the uniform. That's how I could distinguish them from us locals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But whether there were others which were a bit further away from where you were, how could you exclude that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not excluding that. I said approximately that was the number. I didn't count them. It's what I saw. It's what I think, that there were no more than a hundred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you personally observed and what -- and that's what you think they were in total. Thank you. I heard but I may have been --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They rotated every -- one group stayed for 15 days, then they would leave. Another group would come to replace them. It went on for a month. But they rotated, they didn't come all together at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier, I may have been the overlapping speaker, but when I put it to you that the number you mentioned was what you personally saw, that you confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that you said you couldn't exclude that there would have been others which you didn't see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Foca is a very small town. If there had been more of them, they would have been seen. I'm quite sure there were not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic. I'm also looking at the clock by the way but we had a short break and Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the prisoners in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean when I just arrived or generally speaking in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have told us that there were prisoners who were kept by the White Eagles in the KP Dom. At that time when you were talking about them, what was their ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were both Serbs and Muslims, there were prisoners from before the war who were still in the KP Dom and new prisoners were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask an additional question in that respect. How do you know about the prisoners, how many were there and how many Muslim prisoners were there? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say any number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm asking you for the number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I never went into that part of the prison so I don't know how many there were, either said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know that there were Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was present when they were brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many prisoners being brought in did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't stand at the door counting them, I really don't know. I was with my father in his office. The entrance is not really close to the office, so I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When you saw these prisoners being brought in, how do you know that they were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we're coming back to the same thing. Foca is a small town. We know each other, all of us. There were my friends and acquaintances among them. Everybody knew who was Serb, Croat, or Muslim. That's the kind of locality it is. Everything -- everybody knows everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that. But were also Serbs brought in when you were at your father's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that once the Serb guards brought in their own soldier. He must have been making trouble or something, but there were also some Serbs brought in by the military police because they didn't want to respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't give you any numbers. I don't know. Not many. Not many of those who did not respond to the mobilisation. About ten, not more, while I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, how much you think you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Couple minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that we continue the examination-in-chief and -- but I have one question. You said Serbs were brought in and you saw them being brought in. A while ago, you said Serb and Muslims, there were prisoners from before the war who were still in the KP Dom and new prisoners were Muslims. So is that now corrected that new prisoners included Serbs as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes. If I can clear this up, there were a few Serbs among the new prisoners too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have any names of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember. It was 20 years ago. You mean among the Serbs or the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Among the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jovica Kostovic, he used to be a teacher of mine. Aleksandar Eric, a neighbour from my street. Biogradska Street. There were another ten or so. Not many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. The Trial Chamber is conferring. When you were talking about Muslim prisoners, you mentioned the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the Serb guards. The White Eagles were guarding them and the Serb guards were bringing them in?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you said Serb prisoners were brought in by the military police?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a military barracks of the JNA in Foca?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: There was a military barracks in the 1960s and then it was relocated in Visegrad. There remained, however, one unit in Ustikolina. Not really a unit, 20 or three -- 30 men guarding the depots in Ustikolina. There were no JNA troops in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far is Ustikolina from Foca?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: 12 or 13 kilometres. Five minutes by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And at Livade, what kind of an installation is that?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: The old barracks from the 1960s. The old barracks was at Donje Polje with a depot holding wartime commodities reserves, if you know what that is, edible oil, sugar, flour, et cetera, and JNA uniforms were kept there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far from the town is Livade?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned members of the White Eagles and the Serb guards today. How did they treat the Serb population in Foca?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I don't really have a nice word for them. They were really aggressive towards Muslims and Serbs alike. They yelled at us. They -- they were shooting. I really can't say anything nice about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, thank you. That is all we have for you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Before we take the break, one or two more questions, Mr. Krnojelac. Where did these White Eagles and Serb guards come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They came across Pljevlje from Serbia. Because Foca is a tripartite border between Montenegro, Serbia, and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break, Mr. Krnojelac. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first establish whether the videolink functions well. Madam Registrar, I can see you but I've not heard you yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I hereby confirm that we can see and we can hear you. Can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear you as well. Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Traldi. Mr. Traldi is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: This is the second time you've testified; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You testified in the case against your father; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you told the truth in your testimony in that case; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: 100 per cent, and I stand by each and every word I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: During the war, was your nickname Mika?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Mika.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I'd like to look at the chronology of your evidence. You described leaving your home and going to Cerezluk, and I'd like to pick up when you got there. You joined the village guards in Cerezluk; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you first began standing guard duty on or about the 12th of April, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Well, roughly, yes. Perhaps not the first day but the third or fourth day when we moved out of our house and came to our uncle's. But let me say this straight away, we were not forced to do some -- how do I put this? Out of respect for our relatives, we wanted to take turns with them so that they wouldn't have to do it all the time. Out of solidarity, if you can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In fact, it was a relative of yours named Vitomir who had come back from guard duty and you and your brother Spomenko both went to join him; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you stood guard at the water reservoir; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: That's the old reservoir, the old water works, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now you and the other guards had M-48 rifles at this time; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Not everybody. Only Vitomir did. My brother and I did not have a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you were standing guard duty, would one of the other guards leave you their rifle so that you would also be armed?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, your commander in these guards was a man named Dragan Vujicic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, on the 20th of April he came to the reservoir and told you that you didn't need to secure the reservoir anymore; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And a few days before this, what you called in your previous testimony, "the liberation of Foca by the Serbs," had been completed, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Well, we can put it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So Commander Vujicic told you to go to the secondary school in Aladza to get new assignments; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes, because there was mobilisation, that is to say, everybody had to report there in order to be given assignments, or rather it's the Territorial Defence that was established. So everybody had to report for this mobilisation, of course those of military age, men, 18 to 60. There was work obligation there as well, but everybody had to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were mobilised into the Territorial Defence at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were received there by a man named Dragan Lakovic also known as Prle, P-r-l-e; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Lakovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were mobilised specifically into an intervention platoon of the Territorial Defence, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Mr. Vujicic, who had been your commander in the guards, was also made commander of that platoon, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Not that one. I was deployed in another platoon, not his. Although after that, the two platoons were brought together. It was about 20, 10 in one, 10 in the other, and afterwards, it was one and the same platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it was Mr. Lakovic who appointed Vujicic as commander; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Believe me that I don't know who appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, there was an intervention platoon being formed attached to every one of the battalions that was being formed at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I don't know about battalions at all. There were several intervention platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well I'd like to look at one part of your testimony in your father's trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter 31316, e-court page 55. This is transcript page 7410.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Okay. So beginning at line 12, you were asked: "How was it that Vujicic was your commander? Who appointed him?" And you answered: "He was appointed at the secondary school centre --"

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: This is the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Carefully listen, Witness, because there's no B/C/S version of this. It will be interpreted for you. Carefully listen while Mr. Traldi is reading the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll begin at the question again, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were asked: "How was it that Vujicic was your commander? Who appointed him?" And you answered: "He was appoint at the secondary school centre by the man who gave assignments, Lakovic, the one I mentioned. I don't know if his name was Dragan, but his nickname was Prle for sure. I don't know who appointed him guards' commander, because I came there only on the 12th. Maybe he was elected by the others. In any case, Lakovic appointed him commander of the Intervention Platoon, and every battalion had an Intervention Platoon, and we were the Intervention Platoon attached to the 1st Battalion." Now, does this previous testimony of yours refresh your recollection as to whether Dragan Lakovic appointed Mr. Vujicic as the commander of the Intervention Platoon?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I'm saying once again there weren't any battalions. I don't know. I don't see that I said battalions then, either. There's no chance of any battalions being there. Lakovic was certainly at the high school. Now, whether he appointed him or not, I was not present, so I really cannot say with any precision that it was exactly that man that gave that assignment to him. He made the decisions, he had the lists. That's the work he did. Now, who appointed him, I cannot say, but there weren't any battalions. And I don't know how come that is there. I don't think I ever said 1st Battalion because I never knew of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we have an opportunity to verify the audio recording of your testimony where the transcript, apart from the appointment, clearly states that you would have said: "... and we were the intervention platoon attached to the 1st Battalion." If you say that must be wrong, then we might verify that, whether you said it or not. I would like to invite you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to invite you to carefully try to remember whether there platoon was attached to a battalion, whether there were battalions or not, and we'll in any way verify the audio of that session. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, from the secondary school centre, sir, you went to Livade?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that's L-i-v-a-d-e.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You went there to be issued weapons and uniforms; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Correct, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you personally were issued and automatic rifle; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in Livade was in the Territorial Defence warehouse that you went to to receive these supplies?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Exactly. I mentioned that. So the war reserves and the warehouse with the uniforms, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you hear that around this time, there had been Muslim civilians detained at the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes. There were Serbs and Muslims, precisely from my street, from this high rise building. It was called the blue sky scraper, the Serb guards brought them there. Yes, there was shooting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you hear that the Muslims who were being held at the warehouse were later taken to KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, that same day, the 20th of April, 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, could you seek to verify whether possibly he heard or whether it possibly has happened but he has heard it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Going back to my previous question, I asked if you had heard that the Muslims that were being held at the Territorial Defence warehouse were later taken to KP Dom and you answered: "Yes, possibly." What did you mean was possible?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: It is possible, yes. Well, it's possible they were taken to the KP Dom. I did not take them. I don't know. But it is possible that they were taken to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: My question, sir, was specifically: Did you hear that they had been taken there?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, that same day, the 20th of April, 1992, you discovered that your father had been made the temporary warden at KP Dom; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: It's not that I discovered it. My father showed me the decision appointing him warden of the KP Dom, the decision made by the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say "by the board," serving as temporary warden was his work obligation; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Correct, I said board but it was actually Executive Board. Now it has a different name but it's one and the same thing. It's the Executive Board of the municipality. It is the municipality, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you then went to your commanding officer and asked for permission to go to KP Dom with your father; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you continued to go to KP Dom for about 20 days; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Well, approximately, I don't know the exact number of days but approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you'd be there from 7.00 a.m. to 3.00 p.m.; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you continued doing this until about the 15th of May, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes, because I was called up to go to Preljuca then for some activity there, some operation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that in a moment. But before I do, during the time you were at KP Dom, you remained on Territorial Defence duty; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you would have your rifle with you that had been issued to you by the Territorial Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You just mentioned that you left because you were called to go to Preljuca, was it Commander Vujicic who called you to go?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Who was it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Cosovic, nicknamed Cosa, because we were one unit then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that unit was the Dragan Nikolic detachment; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Later on, it became known as the Dragan Nikolic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, when you returned from the front at Preljuca, you were living in the Zelengora hotel with your parents; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes, on the top of the Zelengora hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And there were Serb forces that were also headquartered in that hotel; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: No. No. There were some soldiers there but it's not that the command was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, this Chamber heard the evidence of a witness who was in the Dragan Nikolic detachment, a man named Veselinko Simovic in July, and at transcript page 24392, he was asked: "Where was your detachment headquartered?" And he responded: "In a room in the Zelengora hotel in Foca." So the Dragan Nikolic attachment was headquartered in a room in the hotel, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Well, if Cosa was the entire command, then that's it, but nobody -- I mean only part of the detachment, those who were from villages, they stayed at a hotel. The others stayed at their homes. So if just one man is the entire command, then that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you were being asked in your Krnojelac testimony about someone else, and I just want to pull up that portion of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we would have 65 ter 31316, page 88, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were being asked about a Branko Banovic nicknamed Bota. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes. He was also wounded during the war, he's an invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you were asked as follows: "He was in the Dragan Nikolic Unit during the car, right, in June 1992?" And you --

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We only heard parts of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, the answer you provided to that question was: "I do not remember that unit having existed before my accident. It was established, as far as I know, on the basis of what my friends told me, only afterwards." Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: And that is correct. That's why I'm saying that the unit was named Dragan Nikolic after a soldier from that unit who got killed, but that happened only after my wounding. So what I said is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So I'm trying to understand your evidence. You state in your statement that you were a member of Dragan Nikolic's detachment, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And it might be useful if the witness could be pointed to paragraphs 10 and 15 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please not interrupt Mr. Traldi, because whatever you say then may not be interpreted to us because the interpreters are unable to interpret two persons --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- speaking at the same time. I note, however, that you, while I gave you this advice, that you interrupted me as well. Please wait until the speaker has finished before you say anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. It won't happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So where you say in paragraphs 10 and 15 of your statement that you were in Dragan Nikolic's detachment, the detachment wasn't -- is it your evidence that the detachment was or was not called that while you were in it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: At that time, it wasn't called that. It was named only after my wounding when the Army of Republika Srpska was established while it was the Territorial Defence. We were an intervention platoon, Vujicic and Branislav Cosovic nicknamed Cosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, I'd suggest to you that the evidence you provided in your answer to this question in the Krnojelac trial was incomplete, that you suggested that the unit had not existed before you were wounded when, in fact, the unit did, in your evidence today, exist before you were wounded and was simply renamed later. Your evidence was incomplete in that previous case; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Well, if that's what you say, but I stand by each and every word I said then and now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you said the unit was named the Dragan Nikolic unit a moment ago at temporary transcript page 35 lines 1 and 2. You said it was named the Dragan Nikolic unit "only after your wounding when the Army of Republika Srpska was established." The unit became, in fact, part of the Army of Republika Srpska, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's when it got that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And while you were being deployed at this time in May and June of 1992, you were deployed to a number of places, and I apologise in advance for my pronunciation of them, but the places you were deployed included Repeitor, Zebina Suma, Osanice, and Tjeniste; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Osanice, the relay Preljuca was on that side. They were at Preljuca and they were at Tjeniste where I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Was it Commander Cosovic who would give you your orders to go to these locations?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Do you know who he was getting his orders from?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you said after you said "I really don't know." What did you then add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a private, a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, Tjeniste is where you were injured; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Kosot hill in the area of Tjeniste.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were deployed there at Tjeniste together with Jovan Vukovic's unit; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Jovan Vukovic already had his unit over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he was in command there generally speaking; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: After you were injured, you were taken to Foca hospital; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: That day, yes, and the next day I was transported to the military medical academy, the VMA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were transported there by helicopter; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were treat in the military medical academy for a time and you were then transferred to the Rudo Institute; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I was at the VMA for a month before being transferred to Rudo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you stayed at Rudo until 25 December 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was only then that you returned to Foca.

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: At that time, your parents were living in an apartment in Gornje Polje; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that apartment was owned by KP Dom Foca; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: It was near the KP Dom and previously a Muslim inhabited that apartment, yes. Whether he was employed at the KP Dom, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That Muslim was Pasa Granov, right, who had held the tenant's rights to the apartment?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: No, no. That's an apartment I received temporarily from the municipality and I still live in that apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And that apartment was downstairs from your parents' apartment; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: No. It's in a completely different neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It was, however, refurbished, right, to accommodate your needs because of your injuries?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: You could say that it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you approached the head of the municipal government to arrange that; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Whether he was the president, I don't know, yes, he was the boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when you named this person, you're referring to Radojica Mladjenovic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And at the time -- sorry. Before you moved into the apartment, you went to look at it on one occasion; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you found people there working on the adaptation of the apartment, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: One of the people you found working was a man named Atif; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, he was being held at the KP Dom at that time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he was a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your brother Spomenko was also later given an apartment that formerly belonged to a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were apartments that belonged to the municipality in the sense that the municipality decided what to do with them, and they were inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, part of this problem may have been the result of you using the word "formerly belonged to" where the witness earlier stated that the Muslim had had tenant's rights. Should we clearly distinguish? So I think if you would have phrased the question in accordance with what the witness testified, he would not have had to correct what you suggested to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I take the point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you now about some events that occurred in Foca while you were gone. Now, in paragraph 14 of your statement, you say that: "On several occasions, the Muslims left Foca for reasons known to them and at their own request wishing to go to the territory entirely governed by Muslim authorities." Now, many of the Muslims left while you were not in Foca; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Most of them left while I was still there and what part of them remained left later when I was no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And setting the proportions aside for a moment, by the time you returned in December, they were almost all gone, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: 90 per cent, perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you say in paragraph 16 of your statement that there were platoons under the command of Zaga, Gojko, Pero, Coso. And you say, "None of these were in any manner connected to the VRS but rather functioned independently." Now, the platoon of Coso's that you mention is the Dragan Nikolic unit; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: It was later called Dragan Nikolic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you testified this morning that it became part of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You testified a couple of moments ago that the Dragan Nikolic unit became part of the VRS. Do you recall giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I said when the Army of Republika Srpska was created, the unit was then given the name Dragan Nikolic but it was not while I was there, before I was wounded. Until the 22nd, there was no VRS and no unit called Dragan Nikolic. It got that name afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So just to avoid any ambiguity, I put to you that that unit did, in fact, become part of the Army of Republika Srpska. Do you have any information as to whether that's true or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: That's not true. I was in that unit and I know exactly what we were called. When I left the unit and went to Belgrade, only then did it get the name Dragan Nikolic, by the man who had died fighting for that unit. His name was Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber heard testimony from Witness Simovic, again, that the Dragan Nikolic detachment received orders from Marko Kovac, the commander of the Foca tactical group, and that Kovac reported on the unit's activities to his superiors. Do you have any information as to whether that's true or not?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Marko Kovac was not there when I was a combatant. Marko Kovac was not there at all. He arrived later when the army of the republic was created. He was appointed a commander, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Perhaps it will save time if I ask this way, sir: When you say these units weren't connected to the VRS, are you speaking only of the time before you were injured, that is, up to the 22nd of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm saying. The VRS did not exist until the 22nd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you've said that at that time you didn't know who your commander was getting his instructions from; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I did not interfere with these things, so yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 of your statement, you address the crimes charged in the indictment. And you say: "Anyone who was stronger or madder at any point could have committed the acts which Defence attorneys previously explained to me took place in Foca related to the incidents of which General Mladic stands accused." So it was the Defence team which informed you which acts General Mladic is charged with in Foca; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did the Defence team also inform you that several of those acts also took place while you were not in Foca?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Everything actually happened when I was not in Foca. I mean later, when I was not part of the troops, when I was not a combatant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: With that I'm going to turn to KP Dom, sir. Now, your father was convicted of crimes against humanity due to the crimes that were committed at KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I maintain that my father is not guilty. But he was convicted, yes. And he certainly did nothing to violate any law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, when you first learned your father had been assigned to KP Dom, he told you there were White Eagles there and they were keeping Muslims detained; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you went to KP Dom to protect your father from the White Eagles and from the Serbian guard; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes, because we all knew what kind of people they were and what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And when you say what kind of people they were, they had a reputation for committing crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: The truth is we were all afraid of them, that's right. I don't know if they committed crimes or not. When I was there, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say there were no problems, they never threatened you, did they?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Well they couldn't. I carried a rifle and I wasn't afraid of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you never saw them threaten your father; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Not in my presence, and my father would have told me probably if they had threatened him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: But these same people that you were afraid of were at the time guarding Muslim detainees, guarding the part of the prison where Muslim detainees were held; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the White Eagles left KP Dom before you went to Preljuca around the 15th of May; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And in the Krnojelac case, you testified that by the time you left -- actually let's just call up the relevant transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 31316, page 78. I'm looking for -- it begins on line 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You were asked: "After the white agency else left, you stayed on to protect your father from other people, not the White Eagles; right?" And you answered: "Already at that time, and maybe even earlier, the army had taken over that part of the KP Dom where the Muslims were, and everybody knows what my father did there and what his duties were." And I'll stop at that point. When you said: "... the army had taken over that part of the KP Dom," which army did you mean?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence. To my mind, everybody who had a rifle was a soldier. At that time, it was the Territorial Defence, the TO. In fact, those were old guards who had done a stint on the front line and then come back to take up their old jobs of guards which they had before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And turning to the people detained there now, you considered, didn't you, that it would be hard for anyone to watch detainees being brought in to KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's because bringing a person to KP Dom deprived them of everything; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, let's look at page 64 of this same document, your Krnojelac testimony. And I'm looking at line 13. You had just testified that it was hard for your father to look at people being brought in. Actually, let's read out your previous answer as well. So I'm going to start on line 8, the second sentence. You said: "There was a compulsory work order. The work duty. But knowing my father, I knew that it was hard for him to look at those people being brought in, and of course it was very hard for him to observe all of that and not being able to do anything about it, not being able to help. You were asked: "I'd like to ask you what you mean by 'hard for him to observe all of that.'" You were asked: "What is the all of that that you're referring to? And you answered: "The process of bringing people into the KP Dom itself. You're depriving a person of their liberty, depriving them of everything." Now, my question to you was bringing a person into the KP Dom did deprive them of everything, didn't it, just like you testified in your father's trial?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: When I say "depriving of freedom," it doesn't mean that you deprive people of everything. I think freedom is the greatest thing in life. If you're not free, then what's your life worth?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you and your father knew that these people were being deprived of their freedom for no legal reason, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Certainly some were, but some were not. Those who had weapons in their possession, they were guilty. But others were deprived of freedom for no legal reason, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well let's just go down to the bottom of the same page, lines 23 to 25. Now you're being asked about your father, and you were asked: "In other words, he knew that people were being deprived of their liberty for no legal reason; right?" And you answered: "Every normal person knew that." That was true, wasn't it? Every normal person in Foca knew that people were being taken to the KP Dom and deprived of their liberty for no legal reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would say that this is asked and answered as you can see in the line 23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 44, line 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there was some ambiguity here and there, and therefore Mr. Traldi is allowed to revisit this matter and put to the witness the testimony he gave in the case against his father. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the testimony I read to you or would it assist if I read it again?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: No need. I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That testimony you gave in your father's case was truthful, wasn't it? Every normal person in Foca knew that people were being deprived of their liberty at KP Dom for no legal reason?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that the Territorial Defence had taken over the area where Muslims were detained. The warden of that area was Savo Todorovic, right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he was also convicted of crimes against humanity in the Bosnian court for his role at KP Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: BOZIDAR KRNOJELAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Mr. Lukic, do you have any further questions for the witness? We have approximately five minutes left until the break. If you'd say I need eight or ten minutes, then of course we could consider to continue a bit longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
